item.title: The House That Bends
item.description:
Introduction to Maison Horta

Maison Horta is one of those buildings that makes you stop and stare. It’s on a quiet street in Brussels, tucked away behind what looks like an ordinary façade, but step inside and the whole thing opens up into something that feels almost impossible — a house made of curves, light, and ironwork that looks like it’s growing out of the walls.

Victor Horta built it in 1893, right at the tail end of what we now call Art Nouveau. The style is easy to recognise: flowing lines, organic shapes, a deliberate break from the stiff, symmetrical architecture that came before it. Horta didn’t just adopt the style — he helped invent it. Maison Horta is his first major work, and it’s still one of the best examples of what Art Nouveau could be.

item.title: Enterprise Architecture Resources
item.description:
I’ve been collecting these over the years. Some are worth more than others, and a few have gone stale, but they’re the ones I keep coming back to.

Agile Architect

Application Development Trends

ADT Magazine has an enterprise section that covers the news and trends. It’s not EA-specific but it’s useful for keeping an eye on what’s moving. adtmag.com

item.title: Project architecture is not product architecture
item.description:
I spent a good chunk of last week designing the architecture for a new service. On paper it was clean — well separated concerns, sensible boundaries, tests covering the happy paths. I felt good about it.

Then someone asked what this service was going to become in two years time, and I realised I had no idea. Not because the design was bad, but because I had never really thought about it beyond the project itself. I had optimised for getting something built, not for where it was going.

item.title: Being an architect of the future
item.description:
“We are called to be architects of the future, not its victims.”

I came across this quote from Buckminster Fuller a few days ago and it has been sitting with me ever since. Not because it is profound in some new way — I have heard variations of it before — but because it feels increasingly urgent to actually live by it rather than just nod along.

The way I read it now, trying to figure out what to do with my life, is less about grand architectural visions and more about the small daily choices that add up to whatever kind of future I end up with. It is easy to drift. It is easy to let other people’s plans for you, or the general momentum of things, carry you somewhere you did not choose. And then one day you look up and you are somewhere you never intended to be and you wonder how that happened.

item.title: Enterprise architecture
item.description:
Enterprise architecture is the practice that tries to describe and control an organisation’s structure, processes, applications, systems, and technology in an integrated way.

The word “tries” does a lot of work in that sentence. Most organisations never actually achieve integration. They accumulate systems, outgrow their documentation, and hire someone to draw boxes and arrows.

item.title: Enterprise Architecture Model
item.description:
An architecture model is not just useful to provide insight into the current or future situation; it can also be used to evaluate the transition from ‘as is’ to ’to be’.

The hard part is mapping the gap between where you are and where you want to be, and being honest about which parts of the journey are actually feasible.

item.title: Stakeholders and EA
item.description:
Most stakeholders of a system are not interested in its architecture, but only in the impact of this on their concerns.

Which is fair enough. The CFO doesn’t care about your service mesh. The marketing lead doesn’t care about your data model. They care about cost, risk, speed, and whether the thing they asked for actually works.

The mistake architects make is trying to sell the architecture itself. You don’t lead with diagrams. You lead with outcomes: this change reduces downtime, this pattern cuts deployment time in half, this split lets your team ship independently.

item.title: Enterprise Architecture is the structure and the operational blueprint of a company
item.description:
Enterprise Architecture is the structure and the operational blueprint of a company.

It’s the difference between a building that holds things together and one that collapses the first time the wind picks up. You don’t notice it when it’s done well. You notice it the moment it’s missing.

item.title: Archimate
item.description:
Archimate is an open and independent enterprise architecture modelling language that enables organisations to communicate, design, analyse and manage their enterprise architecture in a visual way.

It provides a comprehensive and consistent modelling language to describe, visualise, analyse and validate the architecture of an enterprise. The language is developed and maintained by The Open Group, the same body behind TOGAF.

The key idea is that enterprise architecture isn’t just about IT systems. It spans business processes, applications, technology infrastructure, and the people and motivations that drive it all. Archimate gives you a common vocabulary across all of those layers so that a business architect, an application architect, and a technology architect can all be talking about the same thing.
